notes.text: No in-person assessments . (1) Students enrolled in Life Science degree posts may not take this course for credit towards any program. (2) Priority will be given to students planning to major or specialist in Psychology. Students across all disciplines will be admitted if space permits. (3) Students who have passed BIOA12H3 will be permitted to take BIOA01H3 and BIOA02H3. (4) Please refer to the requirements of your intended program to determine whether this course is appropriate for your degree. Specifically, students intending to join a program in Health and Society should enroll in BIOA11H3 instead.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Course Title: Economy of Cities Course Description: This course introduces students to economic approaches to cities. Cities are historical hubs of economic life, and economic reasoning has become a dominant lens in policy design and implementation in the last few decades. This course equips students with economic concepts (e.g., supply and demand) and analytical tools that can be applied to the analysis of urban planning and policy.

courses.name: Contemporary Africa: State, Society, and Politics

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Course Description: What does humanitarian aid do? Does it empower communities as it promises, or does it generate unintended consequences? In this course, we will explore some of the most pressing debates in aid and development, from disaster relief and conflict response to resilience, self-reliance, and global justice. Through case examples from the global south, we will examine how humanitarian aid interventions shape people’s lives, spaces, politics, and right-based claims. Taught by Prof. Shalini Mariyathas, a development planner with extensive experience working with aid agencies and communities in war-affected Sri Lanka, the course combines critical academic perspectives with grounded insights to engage with humanitarian aid practice.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Title: Algebraic Topology Description: An introduction to algebraic topology emphasizing the use of algebraic invariants to study topological spaces. Topics include the fundamental group, covering spaces, Van Kampen’s theorem, simplicial and singular homology, CW complexes, and basic cohomology. Applications to geometry are highlighted.
notes.html:
Title: Algebraic Topology 

Description: An introduction to algebraic topology emphasizing the use of algebraic invariants to study topological spaces. Topics include the fundamental group, covering spaces, Van Kampen’s theorem, simplicial and singular homology, CW complexes, and basic cohomology. Applications to geometry are highlighted.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: SUPERVISED STUDY/RESEARCH & INDEPENDENT STUDY COURSES Step 1: Request the course on ACORN. Your status will be INT. You will not be officially enrolled until you complete the remaining steps (below). Step 2: Meet with the MGE faculty member who you hope will supervise your study/project and obtain their approval. Make sure the course code, supervisor name, and title of the project is input on the supervised study form as this information will appear on your transcript. The Supervised Study form is available at: https://www.utsc.utoronto.ca/registrar/supervised-study-form Step 3: Once complete, send the approval email from the faculty member and the completed Supervised Study form by email to the Academic Director, Economics ecoss.utsc@utoronto.ca and Jacqueline Deane jacqueline.deane@utoronto.ca Step 4: If your proposal is approved, the department will update the Registrar's Office with your Supervised Study form. Staff will update your course status on ACORN from interim (INT) to approved (APP). Your Department listed below may require additional paperwork. See policy for more details: https://www.utsc.utoronto.ca/mgmt/sites/utsc.utoronto.ca.mgmt/files/docs/Departmental%20Policy%20on%20Supervised%20Reading%20Courses%20(October%202023).pdf Economics and Management Office IC250

notes.text: Visiting students require the permission of the Academic Director. MANAGEMENT MEETING SECTION CHANGES: Students approved in a course who wish to change sections may do so on ACORN, provided there is space in the preferred section. Section changes can be made on ACORN until the last day to add courses for the session provided there is space to do so. Students are expected to enroll or waitlist for course meeting sections that fit in a conflict-free schedule. Students who knowingly enroll in a course that causes a conflict should not expect to request a section change through their Professor at a later date. Please see Calendar for overall course load limit for BBA students

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: SUPERVISED STUDY/RESEARCH & INDEPENDENT STUDY COURSES Step 1: Request the course on ACORN. Your status will be INT. You will not be officially enrolled until you complete the remaining steps (below). Step 2: Meet with the MGT faculty member who you hope will supervise your study/project and obtain their approval. Make sure the course code, supervisor name, and title of the project is input on the supervised study form as this information will appear on your transcript. The Supervised Study form is available at: https://www.utsc.utoronto.ca/registrar/supervised-study-form Step 3: Once complete, send the approval email from the faculty member and the completed Supervised Study form by email to the Academic Director, Management mgmtss.utsc@utoronto.ca and Jacqueline Deane jacqueline.deane@utoronto.ca Step 4: If your proposal is approved, the department will update the Registrar's Office with your Supervised Study form. Staff will update your course status on ACORN from interim (INT) to approved (APP). Your Department listed below may require additional paperwork. See policy for more details: https://www.utsc.utoronto.ca/mgmt/sites/utsc.utoronto.ca.mgmt/files/docs/Departmental%20Policy%20on%20Supervised%20Reading%20Courses%20(October%202023).pdf Economics and Management Office IC250

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Course enrolment in the following Music Performance course is by an interview. An interview sign-up sheet will be sent to students closer to the beginning of an academic term. To be considered follow the steps below: * Request the course on ACORN. Your status will be 'INT'. * Attend a placement interview - normally held during the week before and during the first week of classes. For more details please visit https://www.utsc.utoronto.ca/acm/music-culture and view the FAQ link. * Decisions will be updated on ACORN beginning Tuesday, September 8th for the Fall Term and Monday, January 11th for the Winter term. notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: SUPERVISED STUDY/RESEARCH & INDEPENDENT STUDY COURSES In order to qualify for a Supervised Study course, students must locate a professor who will agree to supervise the course, and then follow the steps outlined below. Step 1: Request the course on ACORN. Your status will be interim (INT). You will not be officially enrolled until you complete the remaining steps. Step 2: Fill the 'Student' section on a 'Supervised Study Form' available at: https://www.utsc.utoronto.ca/registrar/supervised-study-form Step 3: Once you fill-in the 'Student' section, contact your Supervisor and provide them with the form. notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Course title: Statistical Machine Learning and Foundation Models Course summary: The course studies modern machine learning methods from a statistical perspective. It covers some classical machine learning approaches, then develops probabilistic and representation learning frameworks used in contemporary large-scale systems. Gradient-based likelihood optimization for complex models, variational inference, stochastic variational inference, Bayesian neural networks for uncertainty estimation, and representation learning will be covered. Large language models are introduced as autoregressive probabilistic models trained by maximum likelihood. The course will cover relevant background as necessary. Topics covered include: Classical machine learning: kernel methods, tree-based methods Unsupervised learning including dimension reduction and clustering Gradient-based maximum likelihood for complex models Variational inference and stochastic variational inference Bayesian neural networks and uncertainty Representation learning Large language models with autoregressive modeling
notes.html:
Course title: Statistical Machine Learning and Foundation Models

Course summary:

The course studies modern machine learning methods from a statistical perspective. It covers some classical machine learning approaches, then develops probabilistic and representation learning frameworks used in contemporary large-scale systems. Gradient-based likelihood optimization for complex models, variational inference, stochastic variational inference, Bayesian neural networks for uncertainty estimation, and representation learning will be covered. Large language models are introduced as autoregressive probabilistic models trained by maximum likelihood. The course will cover relevant background as necessary.

Topics covered include:

  • Classical machine learning: kernel methods, tree-based methods
  • Unsupervised learning including dimension reduction and clustering
  • Gradient-based maximum likelihood for complex models
  • Variational inference and stochastic variational inference
  • Bayesian neural networks and uncertainty
  • Representation learning
  • Large language models with autoregressive modeling

notes.text: This semester, our topic is Animalia: we will explore and evaluate the changes in animal-human relationships that took place during this period through critical examination of the ways animals were presented through art and visual culture. Centuries later, we tend to take for granted a narrative that animals have always been part of our world and we have experienced a constant relationship with other creatures. However, the years 1400-1800 saw an important transition from superstition to science, from a rigid and hierarchical view of ‘good animals and bad animals’ to a willingness to explore and understand the diversity of creatures and their unique habitats.  Human-animal interaction from this era is an emerging area in current scholarship, which has shown that this period was much more complex than previously portrayed, and many of the vital topics still resonate with us today: from the visual culture of fantasy to developments in scientific classification, from myths and fables to ownership and training manuals, from images of food, hunting, and pets, we will explore the changes and developments that occurred in our relationship with the animal kingdom during this time period.

notes.text: SUPERVISED STUDY/RESEARCH & INDEPENDENT STUDY COURSES Step 1: Request the course on ACORN. Your status will be INT. Make sure the course code, supervisor name, and title of the project is clearly printed on the form as this information will appear on your transcript. The Supervised Study form is available at: https://www.utsc.utoronto.ca/registrar/supervised-study-form . Your Department may require additional paperwork. Students should contact the Office for more information. Step 3: Submit the signed Supervised Study form and additional paperwork by email to hcs.advising.utsc@utoronto.ca. Staff will update your course status on ACORN from interim (INT) to approved (APP).

SUPERVISED STUDY/RESEARCH & INDEPENDENT STUDY COURSES
Step 1: Request the course on ACORN. Your status will be INT. You will not be officially enrolled until you complete the remaining steps (below).
Step 2: Meet with the Supervisor and obtain their signature on a 'Supervised Study form'. Make sure the course code, supervisor name, and title of the project is clearly printed on the form as this information will appear on your transcript. The Supervised Study form is available at: https://www.utsc.utoronto.ca/registrar/supervised-study-form. Your Department may require additional paperwork. Students should contact the Office for more information.
Step 3: Submit the signed Supervised Study form and additional paperwork by email to hcs.advising.utsc@utoronto.ca. Staff will update your course status on ACORN from interim (INT) to approved (APP).

notes.text: Topic: Monsters She Writes: Gothic Feminism, Transgression, and Rage Madwomen, witches, ghosts, vampires, and artificial beings: monsters have long given form to desires, bodies, and forms of rage that respectable society seeks to repress. This course approaches feminist thought through the Gothic, examining how writers, artists, and filmmakers use horror and monstrosity to confront gendered violence, reproductive control, colonialism, racialization, sexuality, and forbidden forms of intimacy. Moving from classic Gothic fiction to postcolonial, queer, trans, and contemporary digital reimaginings, we will ask: Who gets made into a monster, and what becomes possible when the monster begins to speak, desire, and write back?

Topic: Monsters She Writes: Gothic Feminism, Transgression, and Rage

Madwomen, witches, ghosts, vampires, and artificial beings: monsters have long given form to desires, bodies, and forms of rage that respectable society seeks to repress. This course approaches feminist thought through the Gothic, examining how writers, artists, and filmmakers use horror and monstrosity to confront gendered violence, reproductive control, colonialism, racialization, sexuality, and forbidden forms of intimacy. Moving from classic Gothic fiction to postcolonial, queer, trans, and contemporary digital reimaginings, we will ask: Who gets made into a monster, and what becomes possible when the monster begins to speak, desire, and write back?
